statement: 9 girls and 6 boys come to a dance class. The teacher makes as many pairs as she can, and any two children can be a pair. How many children are left without a partner?

choices.misconception: I thought 9 and 6 add up to an even number, so everyone would get a partner.
I paired each girl with a boy, but any two children can be a pair.
I found how many pairs there are instead of how many children are left over.
I added the girls and boys and stopped without making any pairs.

hints: How many children are there altogether?
Since any two children can make a pair, only the total matters. Make pairs from the whole class and see whether the total is odd or even.
There are 9 + 6 = 15 children. Count in twos up to 15.

solutions.reliable: There are 9 + 6 = 15 children. Pairs use children two at a time: 7 pairs use 14 children, and 1 child is left. The idea to keep: an odd number of things always leaves one over when you put them in pairs.
solutions.elegant: The 6 boys make 3 pairs. 8 of the girls make 4 pairs, and 1 girl is left. Either way exactly one child has no partner, because 15 is odd.

whyOnTest: Odd and even is about pairing, and the girl-with-boy reading is the trap that careful reading avoids.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
